lines: On its own database, a client reading back something it just wrote isn't even a question.
The moment a second node enters the picture, that stops being automatic.
So the real question is what exactly happens the instant that read lands somewhere else.
Commit to an answer before I show you.
A standby out there has already received the bytes of a write, but hasn't actually replayed them yet.
Does the client that made that write see it, the very next time it reads?
answer: It's tempting to say yes, since the client just wrote it moments ago.
But what the standby can show depends entirely on its own replay position, not on who's asking or how recently they wrote.
That position hasn't moved past the write yet. So no, the write simply isn't there.

lines: Here's that guarantee, named precisely.
A process's own write has to be visible to that same process's own later read.
Nothing stronger than that, and notice it says nothing at all about a different process reading the same data.
Watch this actually happen, against a real database, not a thought experiment.
Pause a real standby's own replay. Commit a real write on the primary.
Read the standby right now. The row the client itself just wrote: simply not there.
Fixing this needs something more exact than just waiting a little while.
Capture the primary's own exact commit position the moment the write lands, as a token.
Then make the read wait, not for a fixed amount of time, but until the standby's own replay position has actually passed that exact token.
Run the identical write, the identical read, with that one change.
The row becomes visible at the exact moment replay crosses the token's position.
Not sooner, not with extra margin added for safety. Exactly at that position.
One more thing to commit to before I reveal it.
In every measurement so far, reads off this one standby never go backward.
What would it actually take to make one go backward for real?
answer: It's tempting to think any lagging standby could eventually show you something older than what you already saw.
But one standby is replaying one ordered stream of changes. Its own visible state can only move forward through that stream, never back.
A real violation needs a session that gets served by two different standbys whose own lag varies independently of each other.

lines: That same reasoning covers two guarantees at once.
Reads never moving backward on one session, and an effect never appearing before the cause that produced it.
Both hold here, measured directly, for the identical structural reason: one replica, one ordered stream, nothing to violate it with.
Now put a real load behind all of this.
Two thousand real writes, sent as fast as this connection allows.
And then ask the database itself, not a guess, exactly how far behind writing, flushing, and actually replaying that load left the standby.
Pull the whole topic together.
Three guarantees, and one real fix underneath the one that actually breaks: a token naming the exact position a read has to wait for.
The other two guarantees needed nothing extra, because one replica can't violate them in the first place.
One last scenario. A dashboard reads order counts off a replica running thirty seconds behind, in the middle of a sale.
A customer who just placed an order calls support, asking where it went.
Given everything you just watched measured here: what does the token fix actually cost if you bolt it onto every single dashboard read, and is that even the right place to put it?
answer: It's tempting to reach for the strongest fix and apply it everywhere.
But the dashboard was never checking anyone's own write. Forcing it to wait for the newest possible position just makes it as slow as reading the primary directly, for nothing.
The token belongs on that one customer's own support lookup. The dashboard doesn't need it, and shouldn't pay for it.
